name: Iris Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, parties and government. We sell nothing, campaign for no side, and keep your answers confidential. What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Iris, 43, and I operate a dozer on the waste-rock bank at a large mine. I check the tracks and the bank edge before moving rock, then shape the route the haul trucks use; I like seeing a safe line take form. Wet ground makes me slow down, whatever the schedule says. My partner Malik manages night replenishment at a supermarket, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the dozer crew a faster tally in the office is fine if the waste-rock bank still gets checked properly. I have no reason to pretend a screen can feel the ground settling under the dozer tracks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This would leave my paid shifts and my partner Malik's supermarket wages much as they are. We have around three months of expenses saved, and the mortgage is manageable when both rotas are full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep operating the dozer on the waste bank and writing down soft patches on the inspection sheet. If the tally changes in the first year, I'd ask the shift boss to show me the numbers that feed it before I sign off a load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about work in this picture. I still check the bank twice after rain, because even an ordinary day can go wrong there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened on a wet bank recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The left track sank a few inches near the edge last month. I stopped, called the spotter, and we moved the route back before the next truck came through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Malik's work change at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop might print a neater stock sheet, but Malik still manages the night replenishment crew. Neither of us would change our household plan for that alone.

say: I would accept a **faster office tally** if bank checks remain thorough.
I would say a **screen cannot feel** ground settling under dozer tracks.
think: I expect **both paid rotas** to stay full in this picture.
Our **three-month reserve** supports the mortgage when wages continue.
do: Keep **operating the dozer** and recording soft patches each shift.
Ask the **shift boss** to explain any changed tally before signing.
feel: **Settled** about wages, still careful after rain.
S0.quote: I have no reason to pretend a screen can feel the ground settling under the dozer tracks.
fieldNote: Iris’s **wet-bank incident** shapes her insistence on checking the dozer route with a spotter.
Both current **wage rotas** and a three-month reserve make minor office change feel manageable.

steps.text: Keep paid dozer shifts and record soft patches on inspection sheets
Ask shift boss to explain the changed tally before signing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office buyers and shop stock planners will change before dozer drivers do. I would ask the mine to count safety stops as work when new scheduling software sets our hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dozer still moves rock, but fewer planners might mean fewer standby shifts when the bank is closed. Malik's night team could also lose hours if automated ordering keeps a smaller crew, and I do not know which wage gets hit first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my dozer rota and write every weather stop in my pocket notebook, starting this week. In the first year, if either rota shortens, Malik and I would cancel the children's extra holiday trip and put the saved amount toward mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about a smaller packet arriving without anyone calling it a cut. I would rather have a plain rota than an optimistic speech about efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the notebook add to the official log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The official log shows the dozer stopped, not that two operators stayed on site waiting for a safe route. My notebook would have the hours and the boss's instruction beside each stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Malik ask the shop about staffing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, Malik would ask how many people are assigned to night replenishment after the ordering change. We would compare that answer with the actual roster before cutting more at home.

say: I would say **buyers and planners** change before dozer drivers.
I would ask the mine to count **safety stops** as paid work.
think: I worry **paid standby shifts** might shrink after scheduling changes.
I worry Malik’s **night-team hours** could also fall.
do: Keep the **paid dozer rota** and log weather stops each week.
Cancel the **children’s holiday trip** if either rota shortens.
feel: **Uneasy** about quiet cuts hidden in a smaller pay packet.
S1.quote: I would rather have a plain rota than an optimistic speech about efficiency.
fieldNote: Iris tracks **paid waiting time** that the official equipment log may miss.
Both **mine and supermarket rotas** could shrink, making the mortgage sensitive to modest schedule changes.

steps.text: Keep paid dozer shifts and log weather-stop hours in notebook
Cancel children’s extra holiday trip if either household rota shortens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew thinking AI by 2028 might replace mine planning and shop ordering, then dozer robots could arrive around 2031. I would ask each employer for a real headcount plan before either of us loses hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Malik's stock-planning duties could shrink in 2028, and I expect the mine to cut many dozer seats once robots can push rock. Three months saved will not carry a mortgage and two children through a long gap, and I would lie awake over that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine's personnel office this month for the dozer replacement schedule and Malik would ask the shop about night staffing. In 2029 I'd keep driving the dozer while applying for a posted road-crew operator job at a nearby mine, if its machines are still driven by people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am frightened by the two dates landing close to our mortgage years. I can look at another mine, but that is not the same as having an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a road-crew job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already shape waste-bank approaches and know how to keep loaded trucks off soft ground. I would still need the other mine to accept my vocational certificate and offer a real wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to keep a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first try the mines within commuting distance. Our children are in school, and I would not sell the house because someone said there might be work in another region.

say: I would separate **2028 planning AI** from dozer robots around 2031.
I would ask both employers for **headcount plans** before hours fall.
think: I expect **many paid dozer seats** to disappear with robots.
I fear Malik’s **stock-planning hours** may shrink first.
do: Request the mine’s **replacement schedule** this month.
Keep **driving the dozer** in 2029 while paid shifts remain.
Apply for a **nearby road-crew post** if advertised.
feel: **Sleepless fear** about two wage dates and the mortgage.
S2.quote: I can look at another mine, but that is not the same as having an offer.
fieldNote: Iris sees **Malik’s planning duties** exposed at the AGI date and her dozer seat at the robot date.
Her **nearby application** depends on a posted paid role, while children and mortgage limit any move.

steps.text: Ask mine personnel office for dozer replacement schedule
Keep paid dozer shifts through 2029 while machines need drivers
Apply for posted road-crew operator job at nearby mine if available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years before thinking AI and about eight before dozer robots gives families time to prepare, if employers tell the truth. I would want a paid route from operating into land-stability checks, with a clear certificate requirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when thinking AI arrives, Malik may need to spend more time managing people than ordering stock. At 51 when robots arrive, I will still need wages, and I doubt the mine can turn every driver into an inspector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine training office this year what the land-stability course costs and what certificate it grants. If a paid course with shifts attached is offered, I'd enrol; in 2032 I'd continue dozer work and apply for a posted bank-inspection trainee place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel I could make a careful change over several years. I still dislike the thought of risking a current wage on a course with no job at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a course worth the risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written wage for training days and a named supervisor for field hours. A certificate matters, but an employer needs to say who signs my inspection work before I leave the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Malik do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Malik would ask for a people-management role at the shop if stock ordering shrinks. We would compare both offers before one of us changed shifts, because the children still need a school pickup.

say: I would request a **paid stability course** with clear certificate rules.
I would say the **2034 robot date** allows preparation if employers share plans.
think: I may still need **regular dozer wages** at 51.
I doubt every driver can become a **bank inspector**.
do: Ask for **course costs** and certificate details this year.
Enrol if **training days are paid** and shifts continue.
Apply for a **bank-inspection trainee place** in 2032 if posted.
feel: **Cautiously hopeful** about time, worried about an unfunded course.
S3.quote: A certificate matters, but an employer needs to say who signs my inspection work before I leave the cab.
fieldNote: Iris seeks **written wages and supervision** before taking a course outside familiar operating work.
She and Malik must coordinate **school pickups**, so a shift change affects both earners.

steps.text: Keep paid dozer shifts while asking training office about certificate costs
Enrol in land-stability course if training days are paid
Apply for posted bank-inspection trainee place in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI in 2036 and dozer robots around 2039 give the mine a decade to put a real transition plan on paper. I would ask for road and bank safety rules that a machine has to meet before people leave the cabs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AI arrives and 56 when robots can push rock. Our children will be adults, but we may still have a mortgage, and I have not seen a pension statement that would make retirement safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking dozer shifts and ask payroll for the pension figures this winter. Malik and I would pay a little extra mortgage principal whenever both rotas are full; in 2037 I'd check nearby inspection vacancies and compare their wages with mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady for now because there is paid work and a reserve. I would still be uneasy if the mine waited nine years before telling operators what it planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figure would decide whether you can stop at 56?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension payment after tax and the mortgage balance at that point. I would not call myself retired on a gross estimate when the bank still wants a monthly payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the children change the calculation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They will be grown by 2039, so school expenses should be behind us. I would help them if they needed it, but I cannot plan my wages around a problem that has not happened.

say: I would demand **written transition plans** before 2039 dozer robots.
I would require **bank safety rules** for machines replacing drivers.
think: I may still need **mortgage wages** when robots arrive at 56.
I cannot assume an unknown **pension** makes retirement safe.
do: Keep **paid dozer shifts** and request pension figures.
Pay extra **mortgage principal** after full household rotas.
feel: **Steady now**, uneasy about delayed employer disclosure.
S4.quote: I would not call myself retired on a gross estimate when the bank still wants a monthly payment.
fieldNote: Iris distinguishes **grown children** from current school costs when thinking about 2039.
Her future choice depends on **after-tax pension figures**, the mortgage and actual inspection wages.

steps.text: Keep paid dozer shifts and request pension figures from payroll
Pay extra mortgage principal whenever both household rotas are full
Compare posted inspection wages with current dozer wage in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Malik's stock planning could change first and robot dozers might follow in 2031. Written staffing dates, paid stability training and real inspection vacancies would help. I need actual wages on a page before I give up a cab shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks the waste bank after a machine changes the route overnight. Someone must walk it before the first loaded truck, no matter who drove the dozer.

headlineQuote: I need actual wages on a page before I give up a cab shift.
portrait: Iris is a **43-year-old dozer operator** with two school-age children, a mortgage and roughly three months saved.
She has **never used AI** and relies on track feel, a spotter and written safety records.
She sees Malik’s **stock planning** changing before robots threaten dozer seats.
She would consider **paid stability training** and posted inspection roles after checking wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens Malik’s stock duties before robot dozers may arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing dates**, paid stability training and real inspection vacancies would help Iris.
